title: Serving the One
hook: Guru Arjan sings that he keeps no fast of one faith or the other but serves the One alone (Bhairao M5, ang 1136)

segments.voice: Yesterday, tera keeaa meethaa laagai, what You do seems sweet. Your line was your will is sweet. When something went sideways, did the four words come before the reaction? Day one thousand two hundred eleven.

A street in Lahore or Amritsar in Guru Arjan's day. One neighbor is keeping a Hindu fast. Another is keeping the fast of Ramadan. Both are serious, both devout, and both might well ask the Guru's Sikhs, so which do you keep? In Raga Bhairao, on Ang eleven hundred thirty-six, Guru Arjan answers. He doesn't mock either fast, and he doesn't pick one between them. He names, instead, whom he serves.
screen: `TWO NEIGHBORS, TWO FASTS.` → `WHICH DO YOU KEEP?` → `HE NAMES WHOM HE SERVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the hymn's opening, paraphrased: I keep no fast, nor the month of Ramadan; I serve the One who protects me in the end. And then: the one Master, Gosain and Allah, is mine. Notice the names. Gosain is a name for God from Hindu speech. Allah is the name in Muslim speech. The Guru uses both, for one Lord. The hymn goes on to say he doesn't go on pilgrimage to Mecca or worship at Hindu holy places, and later, paraphrased: I am neither Hindu nor Muslim; my body and breath belong to Allah and Ram. It's easy to hear this as a rejection. Read in its setting, it is a statement of where the Guru stands. Not against his neighbors, and not ranking their devotion, but naming a path given wholly to the One, whatever name the One is called by. Sevi, I serve, is the working word. Service, seva, runs through the Gurus' teaching. And the hymn makes the One the only master of that service. Look back over this week and it's been the same thread in different clothes. The Gatha, dense and short. The Funhe, rhythmic longing. The Chaubole, four voices on a love money can't buy. The Mundavani's plate, truth, contentment, reflection. The Lord standing up to finish the work. Your doing is sweet. And now, the one being served by all of it. Different forms, one direction.
screen: `NO FAST, NO RAMADAN.` · `GOSAIN AND ALLAH, ONE MASTER.` · `NEITHER HINDU NOR MUSLIM.` · `THE WEEK, ONE DIRECTION.` · then, large: `SERVING THE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve the one you love. Bring to mind whoever or whatever your life is most given to. For some it's God, for some a child, a parent, a calling. Hold that one in your attention. Then ask: what small service could I offer that one today? A chore, a call, a quiet act of care. Let the answer come; don't chase it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Serving the One. Guru Arjan's hymn in Raga Bhairao: no fast of one faith or the other; I serve the One who protects me in the end. Today's word.
Your line: serving the one. That closes a week of Guru Arjan's shorter forms and his seal. Today, do the small service you found, and offer it to that one. Day one thousand two hundred eleven.

howItsDone: This hymn of Guru Arjan in Raga Bhairao is often quoted when Sikhs explain their path as distinct and devoted to the One; in the gurdwara it is sung in kirtan and explained in katha.

fork.setup: two devout neighbors keep two different fasts, and someone asks Guru Arjan which one he keeps. what does the hymn say?
options: he keeps the fast of Ramadan.
neither; he serves the One who protects in the end.
fork.reveal: he picks neither and mocks neither: he names a path given wholly to the One, called by both Hindu and Muslim names.

original.note: Him I serve: Guru Arjan's answer in Raga Bhairao, Ang 1136.

notes: The hymn is paraphrased from memory (no fast nor Ramadan; I serve the One who protects in the end; Gosain and Allah one Master; no Hajj or Hindu pilgrimage; neither Hindu nor Muslim; body and breath belong to Allah and Ram); please check against Ang 1136. The text uses 'Turk' for Muslim; the script says 'Muslim'.

This hymn touches two other traditions; it is framed as Guru Arjan naming whom he serves, without ranking or mocking his neighbors. A Keeper should confirm this framing is fair to Sikh reading and to Hindu and Muslim listeners.
The hook's street scene in Lahore or Amritsar is an illustration, not a sourced event.
